title: Custom Steel Profiles: What to Specify Before You Request a Quote
description: Learn when to choose custom steel profiles, what dimensions and drawings to provide, and which framing, documentation, and delivery details to confirm before ordering.
html:
Custom steel profiles are worth considering when a standard stud, track, angle, strip, or channel cannot meet the geometry or dimensions required by your project. The practical decision is whether adapting a standard component or requesting a profile made to your requirements gives the project the clearest path forward.

Start by defining the application, cross-section, dimensions, gauge or thickness, length, quantity, and supporting documentation. A supplier can then review whether the requested shape is appropriate for the intended framing use and determine what further engineering or specification information is needed.

Quick summary

  • Use a standard framing component when it meets the required geometry, performance criteria, and project dimensions.
  • Consider a custom steel profile when the project needs a distinct shape, dimension, angle, return, or length.
  • Include a clear cross-section, dimensions, gauge or thickness, lengths, quantities, application, and relevant drawings in your inquiry.
  • Separate non-load-bearing interior framing from load-bearing, curtain-wall, floor, or roof applications.
  • Before approval, confirm the drawing, specifications, documentation, quantities, packaging, and delivery arrangements.

Standard Framing Components or a Custom Steel Profile?

Standard products are usually the first option to evaluate because their dimensions and intended uses are already defined in a supplier’s product range. Dass Metal Products lists light- and heavy-gauge studs, tracks, channels, U-Flex Track, L Track, and Z-Bar among its framing products. If one meets the project requirement, it may be simpler to specify and purchase than a new profile.

A custom profile becomes more relevant when the required section is not available as a standard product, when a particular geometry must be reproduced, or when a standard component would require substantial modification on site. Custom brake shapes, special profiles, angles, flat strips, and custom-length framing components may be relevant examples, depending on the project requirements.

That does not mean every requested section can automatically be produced or used for every application. The supplier must review the proposed shape, dimensions, material requirements, quantities, and intended use before production is accepted.

Custom Profiles vs. Standard Products: Practical Tradeoffs

Decision factorStandard productCustom steel profile
FitSuitable when an existing component matches the design.Useful when the required cross-section or dimensions are outside the standard range.
Specification controlProduct designations and published dimensions provide a starting point.The buyer must define the shape, dimensions, gauge or thickness, length, and other requirements precisely.
PurchasingUsually easier to identify from a catalogue or schedule.Requires supplier review before production can be confirmed.
CoordinationMay fit an established framing detail with less modification.Requires coordination between the drawing, surrounding materials, fasteners, and installation detail.
SchedulePlanning may be simpler when the product and availability are known.Review, production, quantity, and delivery arrangements require early confirmation.

Price, minimum order quantities, production methods, tolerances, and lead times are project-specific questions. Do not assume them simply because a profile is described as custom.

Which Custom Steel Profile Might Match the Requirement?

Special profiles and custom brake shapes

A special profile or custom brake shape may be appropriate when the project needs a non-standard section made to a particular cross-section. Include a drawing or clearly dimensioned sketch rather than only a general description such as “custom metal trim.”

Angles and L-track

Angles may be useful where the design requires a specific leg arrangement or edge condition. Dass Metal states that L-track is available in multiple sizes and gauges and that it can manufacture angles in almost any size and gauge to meet project requirements. The requested size and gauge still need review for the specific order.

Flat strips

Flat strips and similar steel sections may support unique design requirements or detail-specific connections. Confirm the width, thickness, length, quantity, and intended use. A flat strip should not be treated as an equivalent replacement for a structural framing member without appropriate project review.

Custom-length studs and tracks

Sometimes the cross-section is standard but the required length is not. Dass Metal identifies custom lengths for non-load-bearing steel studs and tracks. State the exact lengths, allowable variation if relevant, quantity by length, and delivery requirements.

Start With the Application, Not Just the Shape

The same general shape can have different requirements depending on where it will be installed. State whether the component is intended for non-load-bearing interior framing, a curtain wall, a load-bearing wall, a floor system, a roof system, or another defined application.

Dass Metal identifies structural steel studs and tracks in various sizes, flange dimensions, gauges, and yield strengths for curtain walls, load-bearing walls, and floor and roof joists. Its light-gauge range includes non-load-bearing steel studs and tracks. These categories should not be substituted based only on appearance.

A custom profile is not automatically structurally adequate, code-compliant, or suitable because it matches a drawing. For load-bearing or engineered applications, provide the relevant design information and obtain the project-specific review required by the project team.

Information to Include in a Custom Profile Request

  • Profile type: Identify whether you need a stud, track, angle, flat strip, channel, brake shape, trim, or another section.
  • Cross-section: Show the profile from the end, including legs, returns, lips, bends, and asymmetry.
  • Dimensions: Mark web width, flange dimensions, return dimensions, bend locations, and critical measurements.
  • Gauge or thickness: State the requested gauge or material thickness.
  • Length: List required piece lengths and indicate whether multiple lengths are needed.
  • Quantity: Provide the number of pieces and any breakdown by size or length.
  • Application: Explain whether the component is for interior, exterior, non-load-bearing, load-bearing, curtain-wall, floor, roof, or another use.
  • Features: Identify required holes, slots, notches, perforations, or other features.
  • Documents: Attach the relevant detail, schedule, specification section, or marked-up sketch.
  • Delivery: State the project location, delivery arrangement, packaging considerations, and known site restrictions.

Do not guess at dimensions that affect fit or structural performance. If a detail is still under design, label it as provisional so confirmed requirements are not confused with items needing review.

How to Prepare Drawings and Supporting Documents

A clear cross-section is more useful than a product name alone. Mark the viewing direction, use consistent units, identify every critical dimension, and show the required length and quantity separately from the shape.

Include the surrounding detail when it affects the request. Show how the profile interfaces with board, studs, tracks, a slab edge, a floor or roof assembly, or another component. This helps distinguish a shape requirement from an application requirement.

Include project specifications or engineering notes when the profile has a structural or performance role. A drawing supports manufacturability review, but it does not guarantee production acceptance, a particular tolerance, or approval for installation.

Questions to Ask Before Approving the Order

  • Does the proposed profile match the latest approved drawing?
  • Have the web, flange, return, angle, gauge or thickness, and length been confirmed?
  • Is the intended application clearly identified, especially for load-bearing or exterior assemblies?
  • Are quantities separated by profile, gauge or thickness, and length?
  • What product documentation will be supplied?
  • Are engineering, specification, or design reviews still outstanding?
  • How will the material be packaged, labelled, and delivered?
  • Have delivery location, access requirements, receiving hours, and scheduling arrangements been confirmed?
  • Are price, minimum quantity, production timing, and delivery still awaiting confirmation?

Keep the approved drawing and final order description together. This reduces the risk of comparing a quotation against one revision and installing from another.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a custom steel profile and a standard framing component?

A standard component is selected from an existing product range. A custom steel profile is requested when the project needs a distinct shape, dimension, angle, thickness, or length that requires supplier review.

What information should I send when requesting a quote?

Send the profile type, cross-section, dimensions, gauge or thickness, length, quantity, application, drawings, relevant specifications, and delivery location. Identify provisional details.

Can custom steel profiles be used for load-bearing framing?

They may be considered, but suitability cannot be assumed from shape alone. Provide the structural application and obtain the necessary project-specific engineering and specification review.

Can steel studs and tracks be made to custom lengths?

Dass Metal identifies custom lengths for non-load-bearing steel studs and tracks. Confirm exact lengths, quantities, and delivery requirements with the supplier.

Conclusion: Make the Profile Decision With Complete Project Information

Choose a standard framing component when it meets the required geometry and project specification. Request custom steel profiles when the project needs a distinct section, angle, strip, brake shape, or length that the standard range does not adequately address.

The strongest inquiry combines a clear cross-section with dimensions, gauge or thickness, lengths, quantities, application, drawings, documentation needs, and delivery information. That gives the supplier a practical basis for review while identifying decisions that still require engineering approval.

For custom profiles, angles, flat strips, custom-length studs, or other metal framing requirements, contact Dass Metal Products with the profile drawing and project details for supplier review.
